title: inference-scrapbook-rowena-2024-09
content:
Purpose: quick, messy notebook for papers and ideas I want to try next sprint. Not polished — reading + to-dos + tiny sketches of experiments. Mostly stream-of-consciousness; thumbnail summaries for later search.

Top takeaways (short):
- KV compression seems the most immediate ops win for our long-window customers; cheap to try: chunk, quantize, store compressed, decompress on hit.
- MoE-style routing for sparsely used long contexts: split cold vs hot contexts and only route heavy compute to hot experts. Complexity grows fast.
- Adaptive micro-batching + early-exit on prefix-match reduces tail latency for interactive apps. Worth prototyping in the hosted stack.

Papers skimmed (notes):
1) "Sparse Experts for Efficient Inference" (sketchy notes):
- idea: maintain many small expert modules; route by key. Win when requests have niche specialization.
- Ops: memory fragmentation + scheduling becomes nightmare on multi-tenant GPUs. Would need a dedicated scheduler (or use Dedicated pools).
- Hypothesis: for retrieval-heavy chat (RAG with long histories), route to a small expert trained/fine-tuned on conversational continuation vs general expert. Could reduce per-token compute without hurting quality.
- Question: how to do warm-start for expert caches when a user returns after days? caching policy needed (LRU vs frequency over active window).

2) "KV Cache Compression and Eviction Strategies" (notes & snippets):
- compressors: int8/4 quantization of KV, run-length encoding for repeated tokens, and delta-encoding for adjacent key vectors. Latency tradeoffs: encode/decode cost vs saved memory and fewer cross-host transfers.
- practical experiment: compress-only-on-eviction: keep raw KVs in local GPU until memory pressure then quantize and push to SSD or shared Redis-like store. On access decode. Simpler than always-compress.
- metrics to measure: decode latency p50/p95, memory pressure events per minute, miss-recovery penalty (ms).

3) "Adaptive Batching with Deadline-Aware Scheduling":
- small windows where we wait X ms or accumulate Y tokens then flush. Work-steering to keep p95 under SLO.
- combine with prefix-KV cache: if prefix hit probability > 0.8 then prefer smaller batch with cached KVs for low latency, else enlarge batch for throughput.
- quick pseudo: 
  if prefix_hit: deadline = 10ms; max_batch = 8; else deadline = 30ms; max_batch = 64
  flush when batch_size == max_batch or wait_time >= deadline
- experiment: simulate with current request traces (sample last 72h) to estimate latency vs cost trade-offs. Need traces anonymized (privacy).

Notes from last week's run (local test):
- ran a toy compressor on a 6B model KV snapshot: quantizing to 4-bit per element cut storage ~3.7x, decode overhead ~0.9ms per chunk (chunk=1024 vectors). For real world this might be OK if chunking aligned with batch accesses.
- micro-batching prototype reduced GPU idle time by ~18% but increased p95 by ~12ms (bad). Adding deadline-aware flush fixed p95 but reduced throughput gains to ~7%.

Ideas to try (prioritized):
1) KV eviction policy A/B: (A) quantize-on-evict -> push to NVMe + store metadata; (B) keep cold shards in compressed Redis with async background decompression. Metric: cost/month + avg latency penalty.
2) Prefix-based early-exit: if prefix matches > threshold and next-token uncertainty low then return cached continuation up to N tokens without recompute (fast path). Risk: stale or hallucination. Need safety checks.
3) Dedicated small-expert pool for conversational continuations: send 20% of traffic (selected by lightweight classifier) to MoE-like route. Evaluate token/sec & quality delta on a small A/B test.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How often do long-session users exercise the same prefixes at scale? Our trace sampling skewed to shorter sessions. Need a retention-cohort query. (Ping analytics)
- How much decompression jitter is acceptable for p95? We have 50ms p95 target on hosted tiers for small chat; decompression must be <~10ms typical.
- Failure modes for cached prefix early-exit: diverging state when model updated; stale cache after model rollout. Need rollout hooks to invalidate cache per model-version.

Quick sketches / notes to self: 
- API: suggest adding KV-ttl metadata for user sessions (user-specified?) e.g., kv_ttl=2h for chatbots with short context, kv_ttl=7d for persistent agents. Could be a tenant-level override.
- Storage layout: chunked to 1024 vectors (align with 1k token windows), each chunk header: model_id, version, start_pos, compressed_size, checksum. Small header helps quick lookup.

Links & references I want to re-read:
- paper on operator fusion for runtime kernels (remembered as something from 2023) -> find later in my notes (TODO).
- internal PR that added batching pipeline: https://github.com/redwood-inference/internal/PR-4123 (linked above). Need to add a deadline hook.

To-dos (next 2 weeks):
- [ ] run cohort query for prefix repetition (request: eng-observability to run on 30-day window) -> assign to Amir
- [ ] prototype quantize-on-evict pipeline on a small dataset (use dev-GPU pool) -> estimate mem savings and decode latency. -> I'm doing this first.
- [ ] sketch API for kv_ttl and cache invalidation on rollout -> write tiny design doc and share with Leah next Wed.
- [ ] mock MoE routing classifier (cheap linear) and run toy routing sim on historical logs (evaluate fraction of requests that would be routed).

Random heuristics / heuristical reminders:
- favor simpler operational paths: decode cost might be cheaper than complexity of edge routing. Start with storage-first optimizations.
- benchmark end-to-end with real traces; microbenchmarks lie.

Conversation snippets (for quick copy into Slack):
- "We can likely get 3-4x KV density with lightweight 4-bit quantization + chunking; decode overhead looks tolerable at chunk sizes of 1k vectors. Proposal: quantify-on-evict prototype this sprint."
- "If we add KV-ttl per request, ops can triage memory pressure per tenant and we'd avoid long tail cold sessions eating memory forever."

End notes: this doc is chaotic by design. Will prune and extract a clean proposal if any of the experiments show promise. If you read this and want to collaborate ping me or drop a TODO in PR-4123.

-- Rowena
